newsitem.title: USA: Using wheelchair, injured Clinton returns to work.
newsitem.headline: Using wheelchair, injured Clinton returns to work.

text.p: Seated in a wheelchair but dressed up in a blue suit, President Bill Clinton on Monday began his first work day since knee surgery by skipping public events but keeping a date with Russia's foreign minister.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry said Clinton was not in much pain from his right knee, which was surgically repaired on Friday for a torn tendon, but said his upper body was sore from a strenuous workout with physical therapists on Sunday.
"The president is very vigorous and active this morning," McCurry told reporters. "His pain has really subsided."

"The knee pain is not that great today, it's really more stiffness and soreness from the workout he had yesterday," McCurry said, adding Clinton had jokingly referred to his physical therapists as "the torture team."
Clinton rushed back from Florida on Friday for emergency surgery after he tore a tendon in his right knee by stumbling on some steps at the estate of Australian golfer Greg Norman.

His recuperation is expected to take months, with about eight weeks spent on crutches and possibly up to six months before he can return to his pastimes of golf and jogging. His leg is immobilized in a brace to keep it from bending.

For now, Clinton is in a wheelchair and for the most part restricting his activities to the upstairs residence of the White House, where furniture has been rearranged and carpets taped down for his convalensence.
"He's not doing wheelies yet, but he's actually pretty good at moving himself around in the wheelchair," McCurry said. "The doctors want him up on crutches within the next couple of days."
McCurry said it was not clear whether Clinton would be on crutches by the time of his summit with Russian President Boris Yeltsin on Thursday and Friday in Helsinki, Finland.

In Moscow, Yeltsin joked about Clinton's injury and signalled that the American president should be ready for tough negotiations in Helsinki. "They said that a sick Yeltsin and a healthy Clinton would come to Helsinki and it turns out the other way around," Yeltsin said in an interview with Russian, American and Finnish television reporters.

With Clinton concentrating on the summit, Vice President Al Gore stepped in at two public events on Monday to speak about campaign finance reform and to celebrate St. Patrick's Day with Irish Prime Minister John Bruton on his behalf.

The long-scheduled summit, which was moved to Europe from Washington because of concerns about Yeltsin's recovery from pneumonia and his quintuple-bypass heart surgery last year, was postponed by one day to give Clinton more time to recover.
Although Clinton kept a low profile in public, McCurry said he had his foreign intelligence briefing and met with chief of staff Erskine Bowles on Monday morning.
He was expected to meet Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov on Monday afternoon to discuss summit preparations but to skip planned St. Patrick's Day celebrations.

McCurry said Clinton was likely to have one, and possibly two, sessions at the White House with his physical therapist from the National Naval Medical Centre in Bethesda, Maryland, where his surgery was performed on Friday afternoon.
Clinton returned to the White House on Sunday and was expected to pursue a much reduced public schedule before he leaves for Helsinki on Wednesday night.

White House officials Clinton would not make a scheduled fund-raising trip to California next week. Gore, who travels to China late this week, will not stand in for the president in California but will pick up the slack for him at other events over the next few weeks, they added.
